sections.title: Setup and quickstart
sections.text:
Arcee • Documentation • Releases • Arcee Open Model API

nac is an open-source coding-agent harness for longer tasks. A persistent direct agent works in your project, can use tools and delegate bounded work to child agents, and retains session history and goals. It takes inspiration from [nanocode](https://github.com/1rgs/nanocode) and [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono).

sections.title: Quickstart
sections.text:
## Quickstart

**By Hand.** Install the latest stable release:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arcee-ai/nac/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
```

The installer puts `nac-web` in `$HOME/.local/bin`. Add that directory to your `PATH` if needed, then start the dashboard from your project,

```sh
nac-web
```

and navigate to the interface in your browser (default: [http://127.0.0.1:3210](http://127.0.0.1:3210/)).

**By Agent.** Nac provides a portable onboarding skill and MCP integration; paste this into your chosen agent harness to install nac, configure it, and connect the MCP:

> Install the nac onboarding skill with `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arcee-ai/nac/main/scripts/install-skill.sh | sh -s -- --target agents`, load `nac-onboarding`, and walk me through installing nac, selecting Arcee login, ChatGPT Codex login, or an OpenAI-compatible API key, adding MCP servers, and connecting your MCP client to nac.

**Upgrade.** Nac ships with a native upgrade function which can be used to install the latest stable release of nac.

```sh
nac-web upgrade
```

### Model Provider Authentication

Pick one before you start a session, or configure it later from the dashboard.

```sh
# Recommended: Arcee device-code login → Latest Open & Arcee Trinity models
nac-web arcee-auth login

# ChatGPT account via OAuth → OpenAI models
nac-web codex-auth login

# Any catalog provider (DeepSeek, Fireworks, Together, OpenAI, Anthropic, arcee-api, …)
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...   # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, TOGETHER_API_KEY, ARCEE_API_KEY, …
```

More details can be found in [Providers and logins](docs/configuration/credentials.md) and [Model configuration](docs/configuration/model.md). 


### Uninstall

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arcee-ai/nac/main/scripts/uninstall.sh | sh
```

sections.title: Contributing
sections.text:
## Contributing

Pull requests are welcome; see [pull request guidance](docs/contributing/pull-requests.md) for scope and before/after evidence. A CLA-signing bot checks every PR against arcee-ai's [CLA](https://github.com/arcee-ai/mergekit/blob/main/CLA.md); comment `I have read the CLA Document and I hereby sign the CLA` on your PR to sign it (or `recheck` to re-run the check).

Development happens on the remote's default branch, currently `dev`; `main`
is not the integration branch. Ask the remote rather than trusting a local
cache, because an older clone's `origin/HEAD` can still point at `main`:

```sh
git fetch origin
git remote show origin | sed -n 's/.*HEAD branch: //p'   # prints: dev
git switch dev                                           # or: git switch -c dev --track origin/dev
```

`git remote set-head origin --auto` refreshes the cached `origin/HEAD` if you
want it to agree; it does not change any branch.

The supported source workflow starts with one dependency setup per fresh
worktree:

```sh
make setup
make dev
```

`make dev` runs the Rust API at `http://127.0.0.1:3210` and the React app at
`http://127.0.0.1:5173`, with Vite HMR and API proxying. Both process trees are
supervised together; Ctrl-C or either process failing stops the other.

If either port is taken, `make dev` stops before starting anything and names
the address and the variable to change. It never stops or reuses the other
process. Pick free ports instead; the Vite proxy follows `DEV_BIND`
automatically, so open the app port:

```sh
DEV_BIND=127.0.0.1:4321 make dev                  # API moves; app stays on 5173
DEV_BIND=127.0.0.1:4321 VITE_PORT=5174 make dev   # both move; open http://127.0.0.1:5174
```

Use `make build` to rebuild the committed frontend bundle and compile the
complete production-embedded debug application, then `make run` to build and
run that production-equivalent application from the current checkout. `make
run` serves one port and uses `RUN_BIND`, not `DEV_BIND`: set
`RUN_BIND=127.0.0.1:4321 make run` when the default port is already in use.

For day-to-day use without replacing a stable installation, install the source
build under its development name:

```sh
make install-dev
# defaults to $HOME/.local/bin/nac-web-dev

make install-dev DEV_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/bin" DEV_BIN_NAME="nac-my-branch"
```

Source builds have the `dev` build track and report the exact source revision.
Without an override they use `dev.db` under `NAC_HOME` (or the normal NAC
configuration directory), isolated from `beta.db` and `stable.db`. Set
`NAC_HOME=/path/to/branch-state` for a fully separate development home, or pass
`DEV_STORE_PATH=/path/to/branch.db` to `make dev` and `--store-path` to the
installed executable. Configuration-level storage overrides remain
authoritative too. Database migrations are forward-only: when testing revisions
that may move backward across an incompatible schema, use a disposable
per-worktree or per-branch store rather than a shared development database.

The local verification lanes are `make test-web` for frontend unit/component
tests, `make test-e2e` for isolated real-browser tests against the embedded
server and a credential-free scripted model, and `make test-durability` for the
focused lifecycle/crash-window regressions. `make test-managed-load` runs the
bounded deterministic legacy load and fault scenario described in
[the managed-load guide](docs/managed/deterministic-load.md). Install the E2E
browser once with `npm --prefix crates/nac-server/web exec -- playwright install chromium`.
`make ci` is the portable unit, lint, formatting, and committed-asset lane.
Run `make test-e2e` as the matching production-browser release gate and
`make test-durability` as a faster focused rerun of crash-window contracts that
are also covered by the broader Rust suites. Release packaging and installer
checks remain workflow-only.

For an explicitly provisioned remote Managed NAC using the legacy BasicAuth
gateway, set

```text
NAC_E2E_REMOTE_URL
NAC_E2E_REMOTE_USERNAME
NAC_E2E_REMOTE_PASSWORD
```

through a private runtime secret source and run `make test-e2e-remote`. This
lane verifies gateway denial, authenticated health/readiness, release identity,
and production-client loading without modifying remote state. Optionally set
`NAC_E2E_REMOTE_EXPECTED_VERSION` to pin the expected release.

For a portal-owned host, set `NAC_E2E_REMOTE_AUTH_MODE=portal-launch`, keep
`NAC_E2E_REMOTE_URL` at the HTTPS host root, and inject the single-use URL as
`NAC_E2E_REMOTE_LAUNCH_URL`; do not set the BasicAuth variables. The launch URL
must use the exact target origin and managed launch route. Portal mode redeems
it once into an isolated browser context, disables trace, screenshot, and video
artifacts before redemption, and refuses `DEBUG` or `PWDEBUG`. An optional
`NAC_E2E_REMOTE_ENVIRONMENT` non-secret label is included with the recorded
build and schema identity.

Never put remote credentials, launch URLs, or cookie values in Git, command
arguments, shell history, test artifacts, or CI logs. The remote smoke lane
complements rather than replaces the isolated local `make test-e2e` suite, and
it remains non-mutating in both authentication modes.

sections.title: MCP in NAC
sections.text:
# MCP in NAC

NAC can connect to MCP servers to give its agents tools, resources and prompts.
NAC also exposes a separate inbound session-management MCP endpoint for external
clients. Adding an outbound server and connecting an external client are different
operations.

sections.title: Add a server
sections.text:
## Add a server

Open **MCP** in the sidebar. Use the MCP Library or add a server with its supported
transport: streamable HTTP uses a URL and optional headers; stdio uses a command,
arguments and optional environment. Enter credentials privately in the product
UI or your own environment, never in a help conversation. Review the server's
trust and approval settings before enabling it. A help answer explains these
steps; it does not save configuration, start a server or grant tool authority.

The canonical file configuration uses `[mcp_servers.<name>]`; see the
[example configuration](../configuration/example.md). `enabled` defaults to
true and `required` to false. An enabled required server whose startup or catalog
fails prevents session admission. Server names namespace tools as
`mcp__<server>__<tool>`. An exact tool denylist wins over an allowlist.
Imported tool approval defaults to `ask`; configured Deny remains effective.
NAC displays skipped server diagnostics when optional discovery fails. A server
being configured does not prove its tools are available in an already-bound
session. Inspect the current session's actual tool list and diagnostics.

sections.title: Connect an external client
sections.text:
## Connect an external client

The default local inbound endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:3210/mcp`, using
streamable HTTP. Configure it in the external client's own MCP settings. The
local listener has no built-in authentication: keep it local unless strong
access control is provided. Managed hosts have their own authenticated routing
and deployment contract; do not assume the local URL applies there.

The separately installable `nac-onboarding` skill helps an external harness
install NAC and connect that client. It remains a setup helper. Bundled
`nac-help` answers questions inside an installed NAC using release-local docs.

sections.title: Availability and backend limits
sections.text:
## Availability and backend limits

The guide can describe MCP configuration while offline. Contacting an actual
MCP server needs its transport, credentials and network to be available. Local,
SSH and Podman execution do not imply that every MCP server is enabled or
reachable. Remote host filesystem paths are not guide reference paths.
If current state is absent, report it as unknown and explain how to inspect it;
do not infer credentials or readiness from documentation.

See [disconnect, log out and revoke](mcp-disconnect-and-logout.md) for the
separate meanings of disabling a connection, ending local login and revoking
provider authorization.

sections.title: Skills
sections.text:
# Skills

Skills are directories containing a `SKILL.md` file. NAC discovers them from project and user skill trees and expands `$skillname` references in direct prompts.

NAC also bundles the first-party [NAC Guide](nac-guide.md) as `nac-help`, including
its immutable release-local references. That name is reserved: a filesystem
definition with the same name (or a space/punctuation suffix that could capture
the same invocation) is skipped with a warning. All other skill names
keep the precedence below. The catalog and expanded body identify official
provenance. The bundled guide uses `nac_guide` rather than host paths.

sections.title: Discovery
sections.text:
## Discovery

Skill trees are scanned in this order. The first definition of a given skill name wins; later copies are skipped with a shadow warning.

| Precedence | Host path | Sandbox guest path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (highest) | `<project-root>/.nac/skills` | `/nac/skills/project/nac` |
| 2 | `<project-root>/.agents/skills` | `/nac/skills/project/agents` |
| 3 | `$NAC_HOME/skills` | `/nac/skills/user/nac-home` |
| 4 (lowest) | `~/.agents/skills` | `/nac/skills/user/agents-home` |

Project root is the nearest ancestor with a `.git` marker, otherwise the session workspace. `NAC_HOME` follows the same resolution as the rest of nac (`$NAC_HOME`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nac`, else `~/.config/nac`). Duplicate host roots are dropped.

Each tree is walked up to 6 directory levels and 2,000 directories. `.git`, `node_modules`, `target`, `.venv`, and `__pycache__` are skipped. A directory that contains `SKILL.md` is treated as one skill; nac does not look for nested skills inside it.

With `--sandbox`, only user trees (`$NAC_HOME/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`) are registered; project trees are not. Over SSH, the same user-only rule applies, and `AGENTS.md` is not loaded. Skill source directories that exist are still auto-mounted read-only into the sandbox at the guest paths above, unless a workspace mount already covers them. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

sections.title: `SKILL.md` format
sections.text:
## `SKILL.md` format

Each skill file must start with YAML frontmatter and a non-empty Markdown body:

```md
---
name: lint
description: Run the project's lint workflow.
compatibility: Optional note shown in the catalog.
---

Instructions the agent should follow.
```

`name` and `description` are required. A missing or empty description or body skips the skill with a warning. If `name` does not match the parent directory, nac still loads it and warns. Unquoted `description` values that contain colons are repaired so they parse as YAML.

nac parses `name`, `description`, and `compatibility`. Other frontmatter, including `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, and `allowed-tools`, does not enforce invocation or tool policy. A catalog's adjacent `skill.json` is not consulted by NAC discovery. Installer eligibility and runtime discovery are separate.

Optional files under `scripts/`, `references/`, and `assets/` (at most 64 total) are listed as skill resources. Activation includes their paths, not their contents; reading or executing them requires an ordinary authorized tool operation.

sections.title: Local direct sessions
sections.text:
## Local direct sessions

A direct session retains its discovered registry at construction. `$skillname` in a submitted prompt expands the selected skill body before the model call. Ordinary prose does not automatically select arbitrary custom skills, and the direct system prompt does not include a general available-skills catalog. There is no `activate_skill` tool. The child launch tool has no skill-selection argument and a fresh child does not inherit the parent’s activated skills. Provide needed instructions in its prompt; explicit `$skillname` references can expand against the child’s registry. Primary agents receive a compact first-party NAC self-help route and can retrieve the installed guide for ordinary product questions. Generic coding tasks merely mentioning NAC do not request unrelated guidance.

Local discovery follows skill-directory symlinks and renders the discovery path as the skill directory. Native resource reads resolve their canonical targets through the normal permission pipeline. A linked package outside the workspace can be discovered and expanded while its resources still require external-directory approval; a link inside the workspace does not grant access to its external target. Hard and configured denials remain effective.

The retained registry contains the loaded body and resource listing. Resource bytes are read from disk when requested and can change independently. Use a reviewed immutable package revision when reproducibility matters. See the [Local linked-skill qualification and supported-use recipe](../qualification/linked-skills.md) for reproducible fixtures, the installed-catalog snapshot, and explicit workflow limits.

sections.title: Referencing skills in a prompt
sections.text:
## Referencing skills in a prompt

In a direct prompt you can reference a skill as `$skillname`. Recognized names are resolved from the session's skill registry, and the skill's instructions are appended to the prompt before the first model call — no tool call and no extra round trip.

The literal `$skillname` stays in your sentence; the skill content is appended after it, wrapped in an `<invoked_skills>` element. You can reference several skills in one prompt: each is included once, in first-reference order.

A `$` token that is not a registered skill is left untouched, so shell variables (`$HOME`, `${VAR}`, `$(cmd)`), money (`$5`), and a trailing `$` all pass through unchanged. Recognition is by name only, so the flip side applies too: if a skill is named `HOME` or `5`, then `$HOME` and `$5` *will* expand — avoid skill names that look like shell variables or numbers. Likewise only the first `$` of a doubled `$` is literal: `$$demo` expands when `demo` is registered, because the second `$` starts the reference.

The chat UI and history show the prompt as you typed it; the expanded form is what the model sees. Resend and retry re-expand from the original text, exactly once — the appended block is never nested.

Every non-empty registered name is `$`-referenceable, including names containing punctuation, leading underscores, or Unicode. At each `$`, registry names are compared literally and the longest boundary-delimited match wins: with both `code` and `code-review` registered, `$code-review` resolves to `code-review`; with only `code`, `$code-review` remains untouched rather than invoking the shorter prefix.

sections.title: Direct sessions
sections.text:
# Direct sessions

The web UI starts a persistent direct coding agent. Direct chats support native
file and terminal tools, traditional child agents, durable goals, Insights,
permissions, compaction, and Local, SSH, Podman or managed-host execution.
A session keeps its behavior after creation.

Traditional children have their own transcripts and generations and share the
parent workspace. See [child sessions](traditional-children.md).

While a direct run is active, the ordinary composer remains available. **Send**
creates a durable `steer` item for the active run; **Queue Next** creates a
durable `queue` item. Pending items show their delivery mode and can be changed
or cancelled until delivery. If a steer reaches the run too late for its final
model boundary, NAC durably promotes it into successor execution rather than
dropping it.

Direct-tool approval authorizes one prepared operation on the session's already
selected execution backend; it is not a sandbox and never changes that backend.
Nested shell command bodies, unbindable redirections, and executable wrappers
are rejected when their paths cannot be authorized independently. Agent opaque
commands and broad shells or interpreters require explicit approval. Empty
`write_stdin` input only observes an exact process-local terminal handle;
nonempty input is a separate one-time approval because the running process may
interpret it as commands. That approval is bound to the handle's originating
session/backend and cannot create a reusable grant. Podman confinement remains
the non-bypassable filesystem and network boundary for commands that need it.
On unsandboxed Local and SSH backends, approving a broad shell, interpreter, or
opaque command authorizes trusted arbitrary code execution for that invocation.
The approval surface states this explicitly: parser-derived protected-path
denials cannot constrain code inside the approved program. Selecting Podman
preserves its stronger confinement boundary for the same invocation.
For the current portable MVP, directly parsed shell path arguments fail closed:
a pathname string cannot stay bound if another process replaces an ancestor
between authorization and OS path resolution. Use NAC's native file/search
tools, or—only when that authority is appropriate—approve broad executable
authority under the trusted-code rule above. Cargo, Git, Make, and similar
project-configured launchers are broad even when their command line contains no
path: mutable build scripts, hooks, helpers, and recipes can execute arbitrary
code. Broad and opaque approvals are invocation-only and never produce partial
remembered grants. This conservative restriction applies on every backend and
avoids presenting pathname revalidation as object-level confinement.

Human product actions retain a separate trusted intent. In a supported direct
primary session, **New shell** and exact human `!` commands skip agent approval
requests even in Manual mode. Hard/configured Deny, authentication/ownership,
configuration and selected-backend admission still apply; agent mode and grants
remain unchanged. Ordinary shell reattach accepts fresh focused typing without
another enable step. Actual unconfirmed input freezes until explicit recovery
acknowledgement and is never replayed automatically. See [permissions](permissions.md).

Explicitly reviewed terminal selections appear as frozen **Terminal selection**
attachments in direct chat history and pending input. Expand source/capture details
to inspect provenance, or **Canonical message** to inspect the exact stored evidence.
Copied text receives no verified attachment. Forked evidence retains the original
source and grants no live terminal access. See [reviewed selections](../terminal-selection-preview.md).

sections.title: Traditional child sessions
sections.text:
# Traditional child sessions

Traditional children are durable, fresh-context coding sessions launched by a
direct parent. A child has its own transcript and generations, while it
shares the parent's workspace and inherits the parent's model, backend, project,
sandbox or SSH configuration, and configured permission rules. Remembered
permission grants are not inherited.

When a running child needs new approval, the parent chat keeps a child-scoped
permission connection open and presents that request beside the child controls.
The child page exposes the same approval control beside its existing-session
composer. A child waits briefly for the parent UI to establish this connection;
without one, the request fails closed and the operation is not executed.
The parent's approval mode — **Manual** by default, **Approve all**, or
**Approve for me** — governs the parent and all of its traditional children.
Approval answers only requests that reach each child's broker after configured
and hard denials; remembered grants remain child-local.

In **Approve for me** mode, the child's permissions dialog retains blocked
reviews even after the child finishes. **Authorize retry** routes through the
owning parent and authorizes one matching child action to be reviewed again;
it does not change the inherited mode or create a remembered grant. A running
child receives a steer for its current generation. A terminal child starts a
new background generation, whose completion is delivered to the parent through
the usual durable completion inbox. Recent reviews and retry authorizations
exist only in the current server process; a restart does not recreate them.

The parent agent starts children with its subagent tool; ask it to delegate
work. The web UI has no manual launch. Children appear in the parent's Subagents
panel, where you can inspect, continue, steer, cancel, or open each one. The
first visible profile is `general`. It exposes exactly `read`, `write`, `edit`,
`glob`, `grep`, `exec_command`, `write_stdin`, and `read_command_output`; it
cannot create goals or launch another child.

The parent's Subagents panel lists each child by description, with the coding-
agent icon, and marks the ones still running. Selecting a row previews its
transcript above a composer for that child: **Send** continues a finished child,
**Steer** and **Stop** act on the running generation. **Open** goes to the
child's own page, which names it a traditional coding agent and returns to the
parent with **Parent chat**. That page keeps the same composer, which acts
through the parent, but its transcript has none of a primary chat's history
controls: no resend, revert, fork, goal, branch, or commit. Child goal ownership
is rejected by the service as well as hidden by the UI.

After sending, the field becomes the draft for the next message. A pending
foreground reply does not prevent steering once the child is running. **Stop**
is a separate button; submitting an empty field never cancels a run. Drafts stay
with their selected child across navigation and same-tab reloads.

If delivery fails or its response is lost, the submitted text is retained
separately from the next draft. An unconfirmed message may already have reached
the child: check its transcript before restoring and sending it again. Recovery
never sends automatically or replaces a newer draft.

A foreground launch waits for the generation's structured outcome. A background
launch returns its durable child ID immediately. When a background generation
settles, NAC atomically records one completion in the parent's inbox, marked
with the child and generation that produced it. If the parent has a run in
progress, the completion is bound to that run and the model sees it at its next
model boundary; the run is never interrupted. If the run ends before that
boundary, or the parent is idle, the completion starts one follow-up run. The
inbox is the source of truth, so a process restart can reconcile an abandoned
generation as interrupted and deliver its outcome once. Do not poll background
children from the model; the completion arrives automatically.

Completions are not your messages: **Pending messages** lists only what you
queued, with its steer/queue and **Cancel** controls, and shows a read-only
count of subagent results still on their way. The inbox API reports each item's
`origin` and refuses to change or cancel a delegated result. Text that merely
looks like a completion is still your own editable message.
The foreground result remains tied to that generation even if a subsequent
generation has already started.

Continuing a terminal child starts its next generation with the same immutable
profile, description, parent, model/backend, and workspace. Sending a prompt to
a running child steers that generation. The description is the label a child
was launched with: a new child requires one, but continuing or steering an
existing child may omit it (or pass `null`) and keeps the original. A
continuation that passes a different description is rejected before the child
runs, with a message naming the original label; repeating it exactly remains
valid. An unknown or unowned child ID is reported only as not found. A parent can have at most four running
children, and the nesting limit is one: children cannot launch grandchildren.
Deleting a parent deletes its child sessions as well.

Parent and child coding tools using the same local checkout share a process-local
read/write gate, which serializes tool-level mutations while allowing discovery
reads to overlap. Retained/background processes can continue after the launch
tool returns, so callers should still avoid assigning overlapping mutations to
independent children. Coordination is process-local; separate NAC processes
must not be used to mutate the same checkout concurrently.

Sandboxed children require a host-backed workspace mount. A sandbox without one
is rejected because it cannot share durable files safely. Approval never changes
the selected execution backend or bypasses sandbox, path, revision, or mutation
policy.
