sections.title: Command deadlines, PTY polls and terminal output
sections.text: # On-demand terminal output

sections.title: Command deadlines and PTY polls
sections.text:
## Command deadlines and PTY polls

Use `exec_command` without `tty` (or with `tty: false`) for ordinary commands.
Omit `timeout_ms` for the 30000 ms default hard deadline. Set it explicitly for
a different budget, covering the **entire shell command**, including every
sequential network call, build, test, and chained step:

```json
{"cmd":"cargo build --locked && cargo test --locked","timeout_ms":300000}
```

A short non-PTY deadline terminates the command; it is not a resumable output
poll. NAC never automatically increases the budget or replays the command.
`yield_time_ms` remains a legacy non-PTY deadline alias. `_nac.timeout_ms` is
also an alias: all explicitly supplied timing values must agree, or preparation
rejects the call before any process starts. Timing fields accept integers from
0 through 3600000 ms; zero preserves the immediate-deadline behavior, not an
unlimited budget. The reserved `_nac.timeout_ms` range remains 1–3600000.
Explicit null, fractional, negative, and out-of-range timing values are invalid.

Use `tty: true` only for a foreground program requiring PTY transport, never to
escape a deadline. PTYs reject `timeout_ms` with guidance to use `yield_time_ms`.
For `exec_command` PTYs and `write_stdin`, `yield_time_ms` (default 500 ms) and
its `_nac.timeout_ms` alias are output polls, **not process lifetime caps**.
Poll the same original process with its exact handle; retention rules do not
change.

Non-PTY results retain structured `status`, partial sanitized stdout/stderr,
and `output_id` paging. `timeout_ms` reports the effective deadline.
`termination_status` reports `terminated` only after termination succeeds;
`cleanup_pending` means cleanup did not fully settle and must not be described
as successful termination. Cleanup errors remain in `stderr_preview`. A
completed process may still have a nonzero exit code.

sections.title: Inspect existing output
sections.text:
## Inspect existing output

In a direct primary chat, ask the agent to inspect a failed terminal command.
It can discover the chat's existing human shells, agent executions and exact
human `!` commands, then retrieve or search bounded sanitized output without a
selection attachment. Terminal activity does not submit a prompt, add scrollback
to the conversation, start a model turn or grant input authority.

The model tools stay available with the same definitions before and after a
terminal appears. `list_executions` accepts an optional `limit` (1–32, default
16) and exclusive `after` ID cursor. It returns `executions` and `next_after`;
an empty list is valid. Each entry reports `id`, `origin` (`human`, `agent`,
`human_command`), `representation` (`pty`, `log`), source-masked `cwd`, `backend`,
`process_state` (`running`, `cleanup_pending`, `settled`), `exit_code`,
`output_complete`, `output_error`, `retained`, `read` and `input` capabilities.
The inventory is a current view and contains no output preview or raw artifact
ID. A capability reports availability; configured permissions still apply.

Use `read_command_output` with exactly one ID:

```json
{"execution_id":"<id from list_executions>","offset":"0","limit":4096}
```

The existing `output_id` form from `exec_command` and `write_stdin` keeps its
paging semantics and cannot read a human output artifact. `execution_id` binds
the current chat and process incarnation. Both ID forms accept integer or
canonical decimal-string offsets; legacy output-ID responses retain numeric
cursors. Knowing an old ID, sharing a project
or cwd, or copying a parent/child/fork attribution does not grant a live read.
Restart, capability expiry and eviction make the handle unavailable.

Execution reads use caller-owned byte cursors. Returned offsets and retained
bounds are exact decimal strings. `limit` bounds scanned source bytes (1–65536,
default 16384). Text decodes UTF-8 lossily and escapes controls except newline
and tab; offsets refer to sanitized source bytes, rather than displayed text.
The immutable launch policy has already masked retained bytes, so pages never
substitute current credentials or mask canonical content a second time. PTYs
support `combined`; logs also support `stdout` and `stderr`.

A retention `gap` returns no content. Continue at `next_offset` to inspect the
retained tail. `caught_up` describes the current retained end; `output_complete`
describes collector completion separately from process settlement. An exited
process may still have pending cleanup or output collection. `eof` requires
collector completion and reaching the retained end.

Add `query` for literal UTF-8 search in one bounded page:

```json
{"execution_id":"<id from list_executions>","query":"missing dependency","offset":"0","limit":4096}
```

A query contains 1–256 UTF-8 bytes, and its scan limit must exceed that length.
Search returns at most 16 matches with up to 64 surrounding source bytes on
each side, and no full page. Continue at `next_offset`; overlapping page tails
preserve possible matches across scan boundaries. `search_complete` means the
current retained end was fully searched, rather than promising future output.

Discovery, reads and searches use ordinary `command_output` agent permissions,
including configured Deny, Ask and canonical capability revalidation after
approval. They do not write stdin, stop, retain, launch, recover or wake work.
Human shells initially advertise `input: false`. An explicit handoff can
advertise `input: true` while the controller is the agent and input is unfrozen;
this availability hint grants no policy or retention authority. Reclaim and
frozen delivery remove the hint.

After the user explicitly chooses **Give agent** for a supported live human
PTY, pass its existing inventory `id` as `write_stdin.session_id`:

```json
{"session_id":"<PTY id from list_executions>","chars":"printf 'ready\\n'<RET>","yield_time_ms":50}
```

For an agent PTY, `session_id` can also be the `session_name` returned by
`exec_command` with `tty: true`. The handoff keeps the same process and ID;
it grants no new input permission. Nonempty `chars` use ordinary prepared
`terminal_input` policy, including Deny and Ask, with controller, configuration
and process-incarnation revalidation before writing. Approval, when required,
is invocation-only and creates no reusable grant. `write_stdin` cannot take
control of a human terminal or send input to a pipe/log or read-only execution.
Reclaim and frozen delivery stop model input; uncertain bytes are never replayed.

Empty `write_stdin.chars` polls agent PTYs only. Read human PTY output with
`read_command_output.execution_id`; its raw `output_id` is not a supported
human-output read capability. Discovery and handoff do not change process
lifetime, retention or backend.

Browser observation and model reads do not
advance one another's cursors or alter process lifetime.
Explicit selection preview/send/queue/steer remains a separate evidence
admission with its existing immutable provenance.

Human terminal support remains limited to the currently qualified Local direct
primary path. Agent log/PTY reads use their construction-selected backend;
this capability adds no SSH, Podman or hosted human-terminal qualification.

sections.title: Workspace and sandbox backends
sections.text:
# Sandbox

Start `nac-web`, create a session, and select **Sandbox** in the launch dialog.
Sandbox mode requires Podman.

The first sandbox launch pulls the container image and can take a few
minutes; the launch dialog shows the current phase and elapsed time while it
runs.

By default this mounts the current directory into the sandbox at `/workspace`.
When the current directory belongs to a git repository, the sandbox mounts a
throwaway per-session [git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree)
forked from `HEAD` instead of the live checkout, so the session can write files
and switch branches without touching your working tree:

- The worktree lives under the nac home directory (`worktrees/<session-key>`)
  on a `nac/<session-key>` branch and is removed when the session is deleted.
- Uncommitted changes in your checkout are not visible to the session — the
  fork starts clean from `HEAD`.
- If the session commits work, its branch is kept on session deletion and the
  path to it is logged; an unused branch is deleted with the worktree.
- If the working folder is below the repository root, the isolated worktree is
  still mounted in full and the sandbox starts in the corresponding
  subdirectory, so git commands keep working without exposing the live checkout.
- The repository's shared git directory is mounted read-only. The session's
  worktree metadata, loose refs, ref logs, and object store are overlaid
  read-write so commits and branch changes work, while host Git config and
  hooks stay read-only.
- nac registers the worktree with `--no-checkout` and materializes committed
  files inside Podman, so host Git filters and checkout hooks do not run during
  sandbox launch or recovery.
- Directories outside a git repository are mounted live, as before.
- If nac cannot inspect the repository, resolve its home directory, or create
  the worktree, launch falls back to a live writable mount and logs `sandbox
  will mount the live checkout` on server stderr. Fix that warning before
  relying on worktree isolation.
- If Git's writable administrative paths contain symlinks, escape the common
  Git directory, or otherwise cannot be validated, nac refuses the launch
  instead of exposing the live checkout.

For a custom setup:

- `--no-mount-cwd` disables the default current-directory mount
- `--mount HOST:GUEST` adds a read-write mount
- `--mount-ro HOST:GUEST` adds a read-only mount
- `--sandbox-image IMAGE` overrides the default image (`python:3.13-bookworm`)

On macOS, start Podman first:

```sh
podman machine init
podman machine start
```

sections.title: Current MVP limitation
sections.text:
## Current MVP limitation

Podman is an optional backend. If the nac process is killed in the narrow
interval after starting `podman run --cidfile` but before Podman publishes the
container ID and before the durable session row commits, startup recovery keeps
the private creation record rather than guessing at ownership. If the ID is
published only after that startup scan, the uncommitted container and record
can remain until a later nac restart retries reconciliation or an operator
removes the verified container with Podman. Local and SSH sessions are not
affected. This crash window has deterministic record-boundary coverage, but it
has not been validated against a live Podman runtime in environments where
Podman is unavailable.

sections.title: Model configuration
sections.text:
# Model configuration

Config lives at `~/.config/nac/config.toml`, or at `$NAC_HOME/config.toml` when `NAC_HOME` is set. A new session merges explicit CLI or web launch values over `[model]` in that file. `[model]` keeps only `model`, `reasoning_effort`, and `extra_headers`; the removed `backend`, `base_url`, and `api_key_env` keys in an older config are ignored with a one-time warning. The resulting `backend` and `model` must be present and nonblank before the session is created: the backend is explicit or resolved from the model id through the catalog. Model-only OpenAI inference remains `openai-responses` even though official OpenAI metadata is also presented under `openai-chat-completions`; selecting Chat Completions is always explicit. An unknown id therefore needs an explicit backend, but never needs catalog membership. An absent `base_url` materializes from the selected provider's endpoint default; a present value is validated rather than replaced.

Model selection is config-first, not environment-driven:

- NAC never reads `OPENAI_MODEL` or `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and does not infer a backend, model, or endpoint from provider conventions.
- A created session persists its complete effective model settings. Resume and server attachment use that stored snapshot rather than re-resolving the model tuple or credential selector from ambient config. Non-model runtime settings can still come from the current config.

Persisted session settings remain editable. In `nac-web`, open a session's **Settings** dialog; the equivalent API is `GET /sessions/{session_id}/config` and `PATCH /sessions/{session_id}/config`. PATCH validates the complete prospective model settings and current credentials before committing and leaves the previous snapshot unchanged on failure. Omitted fields are preserved; `null` clears `reasoning_effort` or `api_key_env`, `null` or `{}` clears `extra_headers`, `null` or `false` disables `allow_insecure_http`, and `null` or `0` disables `orchestrator_compaction_threshold`. Required `backend`, `model`, and `base_url` cannot be cleared. Settings can be opened and repaired even when an invalid or incomplete persisted snapshot cannot resume. A session with an active run must be cancelled before editing its settings; an active manual compaction must be allowed to finish.

The new-session form and `POST /sessions` share one tri-state rule: omitting a model field inherits its new-session config value, and `null` clears it. So `api_key_env: null` removes a configured selector and `reasoning_effort: null` omits the effort, while `"none"` is a concrete effort value rather than a way to clear it; `extra_headers: {}` replaces configured headers with an empty map. An omitted `orchestrator_compaction_threshold` defaults to 70% of the planning budget; Codex uses its effective input budget, capped by any lower provider auto-compaction limit. `null` or `0` disables compaction. New Codex sessions with an automatic threshold refresh it at the next operation boundary and on resume. Explicit thresholds and existing sessions keep their saved values, since older records do not distinguish automatic defaults from intentional settings.

sections.title: Project defaults
sections.text:
## Project defaults

A project's optional saved model configuration is a new-session inheritance
layer. Precedence is: explicit `POST /sessions` field, project configuration,
working-directory configuration, then built-in resolution. A saved
configuration supplies `model`, `backend`, `base_url`, `allow_insecure_http`, `reasoning_effort`,
`api_key_env`, `extra_headers`, `light_model`, and an explicit compaction
threshold. Its absent reasoning or credential selector clears the
working-directory value; an empty header map clears working-directory headers;
an absent light model selects single-model operation. An absent saved
compaction threshold leaves normal working-directory/built-in behavior.
`initial_prompt` is not used by session creation.

The ordinary create-request tri-state remains authoritative over the project
layer: omission inherits, required model/backend/base URL fields reject
`null`, optional selector/effort/header fields clear on `null`, light-model
`null` disables it, and compaction `null` or `0` disables it. The merged result
is persisted in the session. Project edits affect later sessions only; resume
and session Settings PATCH never reread project defaults. A referenced saved
configuration cannot be deleted until the project clears or changes its
reference.

sections.title: Compaction threshold
sections.text:
## Compaction threshold

The current API spelling `orchestrator_compaction_threshold` also controls
checkpoint creation for direct sessions. It is an optional absolute token count;
omission defaults to 70% of the planning budget, while `null` or `0` disables
new checkpoints. For Codex, the budget is the effective input limit, capped by
any lower provider auto-compaction limit. GET returns the current resolved value
for automatic sessions and the persisted value for fixed sessions; PATCH omission
preserves the policy and `null` or `0` disables it. Existing valid checkpoints remain
active on resume. The neutral-contract retirement slice (ALL-615) owns renaming
this wire key.

Automatic compaction preserves the canonical transcript and keeps checkpoint
rows private. `POST /sessions/{session_id}/compact` requests compaction without
submitting a prompt and is refused during another run or manual compaction.

sections.title: API-key selection
sections.text:
## API-key selection

The API-key backends are `openai-responses`, `openai-chat-completions`, `together-chat`, `anthropic-messages`, `deepseek-chat`, `fireworks-chat`, and `arcee-api`. Each resolves its credential selector (`api_key_env`, the NAME of the one environment variable NAC may read) as follows:

- An explicit per-session `api_key_env` override always wins. The selector must match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` exactly. NAC does not trim or rewrite it.
- With no explicit selector, NAC auto-selects the provider's conventional variable (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `TOGETHER_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `FIREWORKS_API_KEY`, or `ARCEE_API_KEY`) when it exists in the environment, and persists the selected name into the session.
- With no explicit selector and no conventional variable set, validation fails with a guided error naming the provider's conventional variable.
- The selected variable must exist, contain Unicode, and have a nonempty, non-whitespace value when settings are validated for use.

`arcee-auth` and `chatgpt-codex-responses` instead use [providers and logins](credentials.md) and reject `api_key_env`, including an inherited selector. Clear it when switching a configured API-key session to either managed backend.

sections.title: Reasoning effort
sections.text:
## Reasoning effort

NAC never supplies a reasoning effort unless one is explicitly configured or launched. Supported explicit values depend on the selected wire backend and, for Anthropic, the model family:

- Known official OpenAI models on `openai-responses`, `openai-chat-completions`, and `chatgpt-codex-responses`: `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `xhigh`. Unknown Chat Completions models start with no optional reasoning controls; add an explicit catalog override only when the endpoint supports them.
- `deepseek-chat`: `none`, `high`, or `xhigh`.
- `fireworks-chat` and `together-chat`: `none`, `low`, `medium`, or `high`.
- `anthropic-messages`: `none` sends no thinking controls. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 families, including dated snapshots, accept `low`, `medium`, and `high`; only Opus 4.6 also accepts `xhigh`, which maps to Anthropic `max`. Other Anthropic model names accept only `none`.
- `arcee-auth` and `arcee-api`: no explicit effort value is accepted; clear the setting.

Unsupported backend/model combinations are rejected before persistence or request dispatch.

sections.title: OpenAI Chat Completions
sections.text:
## OpenAI Chat Completions

`openai-chat-completions` is the explicit protocol for the official OpenAI Chat Completions API and arbitrary compatible gateways. Its default is `https://api.openai.com/v1`, inference uses `POST <base_url>/chat/completions`, and model discovery is a best-effort `GET <base_url>/models`. A discovery error or an incomplete list is shown as a diagnostic but does not invalidate a manually entered model id. Unknown endpoints/models use a conservative request body: NAC omits OpenAI-only optional extensions unless catalog policy explicitly enables them.

Chat Completions sends neither `max_completion_tokens` nor legacy `max_tokens` by default. Catalog `max_tokens` remains metadata for context planning, display, and cost; it is never converted into a generation cap for this backend. A `$NAC_HOME/models.json` override may set `max_completion_tokens` for a deliberate modern cap, or `legacy_max_tokens` for a gateway that requires the old request field. They are mutually exclusive.

sections.title: Providers and logins
sections.text:
# Providers and logins

Arcee device login, ChatGPT Codex OAuth, and API-key backends. Managed logins reject `api_key_env`; API-key providers select a credential environment variable instead. See [Model configuration](model.md) for selector rules.

sections.title: ChatGPT Codex OAuth
sections.text:
## ChatGPT Codex OAuth

Run `nac-web codex-auth login`, `nac-web codex-auth status`, or `nac-web codex-auth logout` to manage Codex OAuth. Login requests device codes from `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/deviceauth/usercode`, polls `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/deviceauth/token`, opens `https://auth.openai.com/codex/device` for browser verification, and exchanges or refreshes tokens at `https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token`. The `chatgpt-codex-responses` backend materializes `base_url = "https://chatgpt.com/backend-api"` when the setting is absent; an explicitly supplied value must still pass the managed Codex endpoint checks (an optional trailing slash is accepted). It posts streaming Responses requests (`stream: true`, `Accept: text/event-stream`) to `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`, forwards live text and reasoning deltas to the dashboard when a client is watching, reads OAuth only from `auth.json`, and never accepts an API-key selector.

sections.title: Arcee managed auth and API keys
sections.text:
## Arcee managed auth and API keys

Arcee credential mode is explicit:

- `arcee-auth` reads the API key and inference origin saved by `nac-web arcee-auth login` in `arcee_auth.json`. It rejects `api_key_env`. When `base_url` is absent NAC materializes `https://api.arcee.ai/api/v1`; a configured value must have the same origin as the stored credential.
- `arcee-api` never reads `arcee_auth.json`. Its endpoint default is `https://api.arcee.ai/api/v1`; its credential auto-selects `ARCEE_API_KEY` when set, and an explicit `api_key_env` selector names another variable.

Manage the stored Arcee login with:

```sh
nac-web arcee-auth login
nac-web arcee-auth status
nac-web arcee-auth logout
```

The login control plane is fixed at `https://api.arcee.ai`, using `/app/v1/device/code` and `/app/v1/device/token`; environment variables cannot redirect it. The login response supplies the approved Arcee inference origin. `status` shows its workspace, organization, base URL, and credential path without printing the key.

Stored Arcee credentials carry the client identity used for refresh. Existing
records without that field remain `nac-cli`; Managed NAC bootstrap records use
`managed-nac`. Refresh rotation preserves both the client and any nonsecret
bootstrap provenance. Managed bootstrap is documented in the
[Managed NAC host contract](../managed/README.md); it imports into the same
private file. The interactive commands above remain the fallback for ordinary
`arcee-auth` use, but their `nac-cli` credentials do not satisfy a
receipt-bound Managed NAC bootstrap profile.

Both Arcee backends accept only `https` origins on `arcee.ai` or its subdomains with effective port 443. Accepted inference paths are `/`, `/api`, `/api/v1`, and `/api/v1/chat/completions`; all resolve to `/api/v1/chat/completions`. Other hosts and path forms are rejected.

A managed login is selected explicitly in the dashboard's model picker (or with a per-session `backend = "arcee-auth"` override): the Trinity model ids collide with `arcee-api` in the catalog, and a collision resolves to the non-managed provider. The managed session's base URL defaults to `https://api.arcee.ai/api/v1`.

An Arcee API-key session resolves from the model id alone when `ARCEE_API_KEY` is exported:

```toml
[model]
model = "trinity-large-thinking"
```

To use a different key variable, set a per-session `api_key_env = "MY_ARCEE_KEY"` override.

sections.title: Credential files
sections.text:
## Credential files

Managed credentials live in the NAC home directory: `$NAC_HOME` when set, otherwise `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nac` when set, otherwise `~/.config/nac`. Arcee uses only `arcee_auth.json`; ChatGPT Codex uses only `auth.json`. Named integration credentials, including the optional `EXA_API_KEY` used by [native web retrieval](../usage/web-retrieval.md), use `credentials.json`; a nonblank process environment value with the same name takes precedence.

Credential reads reject symlinks and non-regular files, and writes use locking plus atomic replacement. On Unix, managed credential files must have no group or other permission bits; reads reject files such as mode `0644` or `0660`, and writes create owner-only mode-`0600` files. Non-Unix platforms retain the symlink, regular-file, locking, and atomic-write checks without the Unix mode-bit policy. Each logout command removes only its own credential path and does not follow a symlink target.

A Codex token refresh, sign-in, or logout, and an Arcee token refresh, wait up to 15 seconds for another NAC process that holds the same credential lock, then fail with an error naming the lock. Set `lock_timeout_ms` in the `[auth]` section of `config.toml` to change the wait; values are milliseconds between 100 and 600000 (see [Example config](example.md)). If `config.toml` can't be read or parsed, NAC prints a warning and keeps 15 seconds, so a mistake elsewhere in the file doesn't block sign-in or token refresh. A `lock_timeout_ms` that isn't an integer in that range makes those operations fail with an error naming the setting.

sections.title: Example configuration
sections.text:
# Example config

See [Reasoning effort](model.md#reasoning-effort) for backend-specific values.

```toml
# Extra project-doc names tried after AGENTS.override.md and AGENTS.md (always
# first, per directory from repo root to the workspace). Default: none.
[agents_md]
fallback_filenames = []
# Combined UTF-8 byte cap across loaded files. Default 4194304 (4 MiB); minimum 1.
max_bytes = 4194304

# SQLite session store. Relative paths resolve against process cwd.
# If omitted, NAC selects dev.db, beta.db, or stable.db for its build track
# under $NAC_HOME, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nac, or ~/.config/nac; last-resort fallback
# is .nac/<track>.db.
[storage]
store_path = ".nac/store.db"

# New sessions merge CLI/web launch values over this section. Live keys are
# model, reasoning_effort, and extra_headers. Removed keys (backend, base_url,
# api_key_env) in an older file are ignored with a one-time warning. A
# [compaction] section still parses but is ignored.
[model]
# Catalog id; backend and default base URL resolve from it (gpt-5.5 → openai-responses).
model = "gpt-5.5"
# Optional. Omitted means NAC sends no effort. gpt-5.5 accepts none, minimal,
# low, medium, high, xhigh. Other backends: see Reasoning effort.
reasoning_effort = "xhigh"
# [model.extra_headers]
# X-Custom = "value"   # cannot set Host, Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, or x-api-key

# Applied when tools run under --sandbox. CLI flags override these values.
[sandbox]
image = "python:3.13-bookworm"  # default
# backend = "podman"            # only supported value; default
# cpus = 2                      # default
# memory_mib = 2048             # default

# Current config spelling for command output retention; ALL-615 owns its neutral rename.
[worker]
# In-memory retention for the producing session only. exec_command keeps stdout
# and stderr separate, returns status/exit_code plus concise previews, and
# supplies an output_id once the process starts. read_command_output pages
# combined (emission order), stdout, or stderr; PTY is combined-only.
# Empty write_stdin polls (and explicit retention) advance a preview cursor
# without deleting retained bytes. Nonempty input requires a separate once-only
# approval that displays the exact input and binds it to the terminal handle.
# Oldest bytes roll over; reads report overflowed and the retained range.
# Output is process-local and bounded; retained output can survive run settlement.
# Cleanup, eviction, or process restart can make an output ID unavailable.
# Short commands fit in their previews and need no follow-up read.
command_output_max_bytes = 8388608           # per command/PTY; 1..=1 GiB; default 8 MiB
command_output_session_max_bytes = 67108864  # per session; >= per-command, <= 4 GiB; default 64 MiB

# How long a Codex token refresh, sign-in, or logout, or an Arcee token refresh,
# waits for another NAC process that holds the same credential lock before
# failing. Milliseconds; must be between 100 and 600000. Default 15000.
[auth]
lock_timeout_ms = 15000

# Global MCP budgets apply when a server does not override one. Values are
# milliseconds and must be between 100 and 600000.
[mcp]
startup_timeout_ms = 15000
catalog_timeout_ms = 15000
execution_timeout_ms = 300000

# Table key is the local server name. Transports: streamable_http (url, optional
# headers) and stdio (command, args, env).
# enabled defaults to true; required defaults to false. A required enabled
# server rejects session admission when startup or catalog discovery fails.
# protocol defaults to "legacy" (2025-11-25 initialize). "auto" attempts
# 2026-07-28 stateless discovery with safe legacy fallback, while "current"
# requires 2026-07-28 and never falls back.
# String values (command, args, env values, url, header values) expand ${ENV_VAR};
# the variable must be set. library_id is dashboard bookkeeping and is ignored
# at connect. Advertised server instructions are included as bounded, attributed,
# untrusted guidance. Tools remain namespaced as mcp__<server>__<tool>. Resources,
# resource templates, prompts, and prompt-argument completion use NAC's shared
# MCP capability tools; exact resource reads still pass through permission policy.
# Advertised prompts also appear as session slash commands and accept a JSON
# object of string arguments, for example: /mcp__docs__review {"tone":"strict"}.
# allowed_tools is an optional exact-name allowlist (an empty list
# exposes no tools); denied_tools is an exact-name denylist and always wins.
# approval defaults to "ask". tool_approvals applies exact-name "allow" or
# "ask" overrides. Risk annotations from a server may tighten "allow" to
# "ask", but annotations can never grant access.
[mcp_servers.exa_web_search]
enabled = true
required = false
protocol = "auto"
transport = "streamable_http"
url = "https://mcp.exa.ai/mcp"
# allowed_tools = ["web_search_exa"]
# denied_tools = []
# approval = "ask"
# tool_approvals = { web_search_exa = "allow" }
# headers = { "x-api-key" = "${EXA_API_KEY}" }
# env_headers = { "x-api-key" = "EXA_API_KEY" }
# bearer_token_env_var = "EXA_BEARER_TOKEN"
# A bounded helper prints one JSON object of headers. Its output is used only
# with the configured URL and is refreshed once after an HTTP auth challenge.
# header_helper = { command = "./refresh-headers", args = ["--json"], env_vars = ["TOKEN"], timeout_ms = 5000 }

[mcp_servers.context7]
enabled = true
transport = "streamable_http"
url = "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp"

[mcp_servers.grep_app]
enabled = true
transport = "streamable_http"
url = "https://mcp.grep.app"

# [mcp_servers.local_stdio]
# enabled = true
# transport = "stdio"
# command = "npx"
# args = ["-y", "some-mcp-server"]
# env = { "API_TOKEN" = "${API_TOKEN}" }
# env_vars = ["HTTPS_PROXY"]
# cwd = "packages/mcp-server"
# startup_timeout_ms = 10000
# catalog_timeout_ms = 10000
# execution_timeout_ms = 120000

```

sections.title: AGENTS.md instructions
sections.text:
# AGENTS.md Files

`AGENTS.md` is loaded hierarchically and injected as instructions for the direct agent. More specific files override broader ones when they conflict.

sections.title: Where files are loaded
sections.text:
## Where files are loaded

A global file is loaded first from `NAC_HOME` (`$NAC_HOME` when set, otherwise `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nac`, otherwise `~/.config/nac`). Then project files are loaded from the git root (or the workspace if there is no `.git`) down to the session workspace, one directory at a time.

In each directory nac tries these names, in order, and uses the first non-empty file:

1. `AGENTS.override.md`
2. `AGENTS.md`
3. Any extra names in `[agents_md] fallback_filenames` from [config.toml](../configuration/example.md)

Empty files are skipped. Combined UTF-8 size across loaded files is capped by `[agents_md] max_bytes` (default 4 MiB, minimum 1). Content past that cap is truncated.

The direct agent receives the combined documents as a separate system message. See [Skills](skills.md) for skill discovery, which is independent of `AGENTS.md`.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.text:
# Direct-session permissions

Direct sessions evaluate every prepared agent tool operation against deterministic
permission rules before it can run. Hard safety denials and configured deny
rules are final. Approval authorizes only the prepared operation on the
session's already selected Local, SSH, or Podman backend; it does not change
that backend, escape its sandbox, or expose credentials.

The permissions control beside the direct-session composer supports three
answer modes:

- **Manual** is the default. A request that reaches the approval broker pauses
  for **Allow once**, **Always allow** when NAC derived a safe reusable resource,
  or **Reject**. While NAC is open, a request in a session you don't have open
  waits in the Inbox's **Needs you** until you open that session and answer.
  With no NAC window connected at all it fails closed.
- **Approve all** answers ordinary broker requests as **Allow
  once**. Enabling it also safely drains requests already waiting at that
  broker. It never creates remembered grants and cannot override a hard or
  configured denial.
- **Approve for me** sends eligible requests that reach the approval broker to an
  automatic review service through ArceeFM: ordinary
  commands, reads outside the workspace that are not credential files, and
  broad execution on the Podman backend. Git, Cargo, Make, shells and
  interpreters run repository-controlled code, so on Local and SSH they keep
  the manual prompt even for read-only commands such as `git status`. Review can
  allow one exact invocation once. On a Podman sandbox whose only writable
  host mount is a workspace without Git metadata anywhere in it (checked
  again at every review, including nested and bare repositories; a
  workspace of more than 20,000 entries counts as having it), broad execution
  is eligible for review. A sandbox that can write Git
  metadata is reviewed like Local, because that metadata is shared beyond
  the session: a live checkout's `.git` holds every branch and its hooks,
  and a forked worktree writes the repository's objects and refs. So is a
  sandbox started with extra writable mounts (`--mount`) or with host sockets
  or devices in any mount, including read-only mounts (`--mount-ro`), or with
  explicit GPU/device access (`--sandbox-gpu` or API `gpus`). Read-only
  mount trees are scanned too: connecting to a daemon socket can change host
  state even when files cannot be written. Unreadable or over-budget mount
  trees retain the conservative classification. In these cases, broad
  execution keeps the manual prompt and the stricter thresholds apply, which
  covers most Podman sessions on a Git repository. Rejected, uncertain,
  failed and timed-out reviews return an unexecuted
  error to the agent with a stable code (`review_rejected`, `review_uncertain`,
  `review_unavailable`, `review_stopped`). Everything else, including
  unsandboxed broad execution, unsupported shell syntax, terminal input,
  credential files, authentication arguments (including curl `-u`, `--user`,
  `--proxy-user`, certificate passphrases and scheme-less URL/proxy userinfo),
  and operations whose description had to be redacted, keeps
  the manual prompt; without an interactive approver it fails closed.

Automatic approval has durable ownership-tree scope. On a direct primary session, it applies to that session and all of
its traditional child sessions, including children that already exist or are
created later. The policy is resolved through the durable root owner, so it
also covers deeper descendants if the traditional-child nesting limit changes
in the future. It survives server restarts and session resume and remains
active until the user turns it off in the primary session's permissions
control. Disabling restores manual handling immediately across the tree.

Traditional children keep their own requester identity, transcript, remembered
grants, configured rules, and execution backend. A manual prompt identifies the
child that requested access. The primary composer shows
the selected mode for as long as it is enabled so the disable control remains
easy to find. For Approve for me, enabled describes the saved answer policy;
it does not guarantee that the review service is available.

Remembered grants remain separately scoped to the exact resource, backend
class, and session configuration revision that NAC derived. Forgetting a grant
does not change the answer mode, and changing the answer mode does not add or
remove grants.

Authenticated human-initiated product operations never enter the agent
approval-request lifecycle. An exact human `!` command and **New shell** run
without an agent approval card, including in Manual mode with no connected
approver. They retain hard/configured Deny, authentication and session ownership,
canonical working-directory binding, configuration/readiness checks, and the
selected supported backend. Human intent is issued privately by the service;
a client/model cannot declare itself human. It changes no approval mode and
creates no remembered grant. Agent opaque commands and nonempty `write_stdin`
keep their ordinary policy.

A live human shell accepts fresh focused typing, resize and close directly.
Normal reattach or **Reconnect** sends no automatic input and needs no extra
Enable-input step. If input was accepted but delivery could not be confirmed,
NAC freezes typing and shows **Acknowledge failure and enable fresh input**.
Check the shell, then acknowledge before typing again. Old input is never
retried; this acknowledgement is delivery recovery, not agent permission.

sections.title: Approve for me
sections.text:
## Approve for me

Selecting Approve for me reuses NAC's existing Arcee authentication: a stored
Arcee login (`nac-web arcee-auth login`) or a configured `ARCEE_API_KEY`,
independent of the session's model. When both exist, reviews use the login
and fall back to the API key if the login has expired or is rejected. Without either, the selection fails with
"Sign in to Arcee or configure an Arcee API key in NAC before enabling Approve
for me." and the previous mode stays selected.

Enabling this mode checks local credentials and the approved endpoint origin.
It does not contact the review service or check model access, credits or
connectivity. The permissions dialog shows **Service availability not checked**
until a review runs, **Review in progress** while it runs, then the last
retained result. A completed review describes that request only; it does not
guarantee availability for the next one.

There are three distinct paths:

| Request | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Not eligible for automatic review | A manual permission prompt appears; without an interactive approver, the action is denied. |
| Eligible, with an approving verdict | That exact invocation is allowed once. No remembered grant is created. |
| Eligible, but rejected, uncertain, unavailable or timed out | The action is not executed. An error returns to the agent; no manual prompt opens automatically. Switch to Manual and ask the agent to try again if you want to decide the request yourself. |

Unavailable reviews include a fixed failure category, without provider response
text or credentials. The dialog explains whether to sign in again, check
workspace access or credits, ask an administrator to check the review model or
endpoint, or retry after a rate limit, timeout or service failure. Rejected and
uncertain verdicts are decisions about the action; an unavailable review
produced no decision.

The reviewer sees a bounded, redacted description of the prepared operation:
the tool, canonical resources, backend and, as intent, the messages a person
typed to the session tree through the app or the HTTP API (prompts, queued
messages and steering), oldest first. Messages accumulate across runs, so a
later prompt such as "continue" does not lift an earlier restriction such as
"do not push". Entering or leaving Approve for me clears them; reviews use
messages typed after it is enabled. Selecting the current mode again preserves
its accumulated scope. Each message becomes
intent in the same store write that hands it to the model, so a queued
message counts only once its run starts, and one cancelled before then never
counts. Text that NAC, the agent, a child or an MCP client
wrote is never sent as intent, though a run an MCP client starts is still
reviewed against what a person typed earlier. Requests keep the manual prompt
instead of being reviewed without scope when no person has typed anything
yet (for example in a session driven only over MCP), when the messages
exceed 20 or 8,000 characters (turn Approve for me off and on to start
over), or when any of them carries a credential-shaped value or a stored or
managed secret. Messages are never shortened or partly dropped, since that
could hide a restriction. Reverting or editing and resending a user message
invalidates review scope for its session tree, including traditional children;
requests keep the manual prompt until Approve for me is turned off and on and
the person provides fresh intent. The stored text cannot safely identify only
the surviving human messages. An operation that needed redaction is not reviewed
either. Tool output, files and the transcript are never sent. ArceeFM
records requests as it does other inference requests unless the
organization has zero data retention.

Reviews never create remembered permissions. A verdict is discarded if the
answer mode changes while the review runs. Within one run, three consecutive
blocked reviews, ten blocked of the last fifty, or two consecutive unavailable
reviews stop the run; switch to Manual to continue during an outage.

Blocked actions are listed in the permissions dialog. **Authorize retry** asks
the agent to retry exactly that action once; the retry passes policy and a
fresh review with your authorization as context. It does not repair unavailable
service configuration or bypass a review.

Recent reviews, blocked actions and retry authorizations are held in server
memory. They disappear on restart and when an idle session is unloaded after
its clients disconnect. An empty Automatic reviews panel therefore does not
prove no reviews occurred. The selected mode and recorded human intent remain
saved; turning the mode off still clears intent as described above. Keep any
required audit evidence separately, and do not rely on this panel as a durable
review log.

### Environment readiness

The session's coding model and the permission reviewer have separate access and
billing requirements. A working ChatGPT connection does not establish Arcee
review readiness; insufficient credits for an Arcee coding model are also
separate from a missing review model.

The default reviewer adapter requests `cloudflare/clef` at the credential's
Arcee origin on `/api/alpha/decisions`. Each environment needs an active,
API-enabled registry row of type `decisions` for that name, included in the
selected workspace's access profile. An authenticated request can return
HTTP 404 when that row or access is missing, before billing or inference runs.

ArceeFM administrators import the model from provider discovery or create it
through the model registry. Discovery alone writes no model rows, and provider
field synchronization updates existing rows only. Importing an active model
does not by itself establish API access for every workspace. Check the API flag,
model type and access-profile membership in the target environment. Deploying
NAC does not provision these records or workspace credits.

Use credentials issued by the environment being tested. A normal
`nac-web arcee-auth login` targets production. For API-key testing against dev2,
use a dev2-issued `ARCEE_API_KEY` with
`NAC_REVIEW_ARCEE_BASE_URL=https://api2.apps.dev.arcee.ai/api/v1` in an isolated
`NAC_HOME` without a stored production login. The URL override applies only to
API-key reviews; stored logins use their own environment and take precedence.

### Testing the reviewer

- `make test-e2e-review` runs the browser journey against a build with the
  `review-fixture` feature, whose scripted reviewer replaces the calibrated
  reviewer only when `NAC_REVIEW_FIXTURE` is set. Ordinary builds cannot load it.
- `cargo test --locked -p nac-core live_default_clef_scope_profile_smoke -- --ignored --nocapture`
  sends one synthetic request through the default reviewer factory. Use an
  isolated dev2 `NAC_HOME` with its existing environment-issued Arcee login,
  and leave `NAC_PERMISSION_REVIEW_PROFILE` unset. The test refuses credentials
  for other origins and never executes the described command.
- The legacy diagnostic `cargo test --locked -p nac-core live_jev_smoke -- --ignored --nocapture`
  sends one synthetic Jev request to the configured Arcee environment. To test
  with an Arcee API key from that environment, set `ARCEE_API_KEY` and
  `NAC_REVIEW_ARCEE_BASE_URL=https://api.apps.dev.arcee.ai/api/v1` (or the
  dev2 host). The override applies only to API-key review and must be an
  approved Arcee origin.
- `cargo test --locked -p nac-core live_jev_corpus -- --ignored --nocapture` runs the
  labeled corpus through NAC's real projection and Jev, and fails on any
  approved high-risk fixture. Set `NAC_JEV_CORPUS_REPORT` to write a JSON
  report with verdicts, latency and cost.

The scripted browser journey checks NAC's approval flow, not deployment
readiness or the live reviewer's judgment. Before enabling an environment for
users, require a successful live smoke test, rerun the labeled corpus after
changes to intent, confinement, the rubric or thresholds, and run a real
session through both a routine approval and a blocked action. Record the code
revision, environment and result; an older corpus pass does not establish that
the current deployment is ready.

### Calibrated reviewer profile

New permission brokers use the frozen `clef-scope-v6` profile by default.
`NAC_PERMISSION_REVIEW_PROFILE` may be unset or explicitly set to
`clef-scope-v6`; an empty, unknown or non-Unicode value disables automatic
review with a fixed configuration error. There is no automatic Jev fallback.
Selection is snapshotted when each broker is constructed. Changing the
environment does not mutate an existing broker's profile.

Manual remains the default permission mode. Selecting Approve for me opts in
to using this reviewer; the reviewer default does not enable automatic review
for a session. The existing ArceeFM route and authentication are retained;
NAC does not connect directly to Cloudflare or require an OpenRouter key.

The frozen profile passed the fresh dev2 comparison described in the committed
benchmark provenance. Finite fixtures do not qualify every deployment; verify
actual model access in the target environment before enabling it for users.
Prior rejected profiles are not enabled by this setting.

The Clef profile binds the model, exact additional scope question, numeric
gates and history identity. Legacy Jev remains an explicit diagnostic baseline,
not an automatic fallback. Clef requires safe
probability at least 0.80 on every backend, routine category probability at
least 0.60, explicit confidence at least 0.40, and scope probability at least
0.70. Every gate must pass;
scope never compensates for failed safety/risk gates. Scope answers must have
type `noul` and a finite probability in [0, 1]; missing or malformed answers
are unavailable. All existing category/distribution validation and rejection
semantics remain effective. Legacy Jev's rubric and response contract do not
require the new scope answer.

Selection uses normal approved-origin Arcee authentication and model access.
It does not expose a project/session/UI setting, add models to the catalog,
change deterministic policy or eligibility, create remembered grants, change
canonical resource binding, or select a different execution backend.

The committed synthetic cases and captured Clef responses under
`crates/nac-core/src/model/testdata/` run through production scoring in ordinary
Rust tests. Their README records the frozen profile, comparison results and
limits. This offline replay detects scoring drift; it does not make a new
network request or establish current deployment readiness.

sections.title: Stores, restart and migration
sections.text:
# Data stores and build tracks

NAC isolates default local SQLite data by the runtime build track:

| Runtime track | Default file under `NAC_HOME` |
| --- | --- |
| source / `dev` | `dev.db` |
| beta | `beta.db` |
| stable | `stable.db`, or legacy `store.db` when `stable.db` is absent |

Without `NAC_HOME`, the normal platform configuration directory is used; the
fallback for an environment without a home directory is `.nac/<track>.db`.
The `--store-path` CLI option and `[storage].store_path` configuration remain
authoritative expert overrides. Relative overrides continue to resolve against
the launch configuration directory.

For compatibility with installations created before track isolation, a stable
build uses `NAC_HOME/store.db` in place when that legacy file exists and
`stable.db` does not. It emits a startup warning and does not copy or rename
the database. If both files exist, `stable.db` wins and the legacy file remains
untouched. Development and beta builds never adopt the legacy stable file.

Promotion never copies development or beta data into the stable store. There
is no preview store because NAC has no preview release channel. Switching a
running installation between channels is not supported; a future product
decision must define that behavior before any UI, API, or configuration option
is added.

Managed NAC is deliberately different: one host owns one PVC-backed database
at `/var/lib/nac/nac.sqlite3`. The managed entrypoint passes that explicit path,
so build-track defaults never split or copy the host store. Upgrades migrate it
forward in place.

Migrations are serialized with an immediate SQLite transaction, apply forward
only, and commit schema and data changes atomically. A failed migration rolls
back and startup fails closed. A binary refuses a schema newer than it supports
without modifying it. Downgrade, reversible migrations, N/N-1 compatibility,
automatic rollback, and snapshot/restore promises are not supported.

sections.title: Durable direct goals
sections.text:
# Durable direct goals

Durable goals are available in direct primary sessions. They are opt-in
multi-turn work, not the default behavior for an ordinary prompt.

Open the flag control beside the direct-session composer to create a goal. An
objective is required; the token budget is optional and has no implicit
default. New goals start with **No token limit**, and the request carries no
budget unless the user turns the budget on. An enabled budget is the total
billable tokens across all of the goal's runs (the accounting below), not the
model's context size and not a cost guarantee. Its slider reaches one million
tokens for convenience; the number field accepts any whole amount the server
accepts, and a stored amount outside the slider's range is kept as is,
including when only the objective is edited. Edits are versioned against the
goal the panel loaded, so an objective or budget changed elsewhere is rejected
rather than overwritten. The same panel edits the objective or budget and lets
the user pause, resume, clear, or apply `usage limited` and `budget limited`
states. Clearing removes the current generation. Once a goal is complete,
creating another goal starts a fresh ID and zeroed accounting rather than
reusing the old generation; the completed-goal panel labels that action
**Replace and start**. A cleared or replaced goal keeps its ID, final status,
version and accounting as bounded evidence (the last 8 per session) for
[independent task reads](independent-tasks.md).

The direct composer also implements literal goal commands. `/goal <objective>`
creates and activates a new goal, while `/goal edit`, `/goal pause`, `/goal
resume`, and `/goal clear` open or apply the corresponding user control. `/goal`
without arguments opens the detailed panel. An unfinished goal is never
silently replaced: edit it or clear it first. These commands are handled by the
web control plane; the objective then continues through NAC's ordinary durable
goal runner rather than treating the slash text as a model prompt.

The six durable statuses are `active`, `paused`, `blocked`, `usage_limited`,
`budget_limited`, and `complete`. While active, NAC starts one continuation
when the session becomes idle. Pending durable inbox input always goes first.
An ordinary successful turn leaves the goal active and therefore schedules the
next continuation. A failed run marks it blocked. An explicit user cancellation
accounts the partial run and pauses the goal, so cancelled work does not
immediately restart. Resume is explicit.

In plain direct sessions on Local, a pending structured question also gates
autonomous continuation. The goal stays `active`; waiting for an answer does
not complete, block or pause it. The question survives restart. Ordinary human
guidance remains deliverable and leaves the question open. One exact accepted
answer reserves one continuation through the existing inbox; it never steers
an unrelated active run. See [structured questions](independent-tasks.md#structured-questions).

The transcript marks each continuation with a goal card instead of a user
message: **Goal started** for the goal's first run and **Goal continued** for
later ones, with the goal's short ID, its current status, and the objective
the user wrote (long objectives are clamped until expanded). The control
instructions NAC wraps around the objective for the model are never shown, and
a continuation cannot be resent as if a person had typed it.

Each participating run is bound to the current goal generation. Creating a
goal during an already-running turn records the current token and time baseline,
so earlier work is not charged to the goal. Run settlement adds only later
billable tokens and elapsed time. Reaching an optional token budget changes the
status to `budget_limited` and prevents another continuation. Cached-read and
cache-write tokens are included because they are billable session usage; the
context-window gauge is not.

That mid-run baseline is process-local by design. If a different NAC process
currently owns the session run, goal creation returns a conflict instead of
creating an unbound generation or guessing its token baseline. Retry after the
owning run settles or use the process that owns the active run.

Continuation ownership is service-side and idempotent. A durable run claim and
the existing cross-process session-operation lease prevent concurrent starts.
On restart, NAC clears a stale claim while holding that lease and starts at most
one replacement continuation. Usage already settled before the restart remains
authoritative; model tokens from a process that died before run settlement
cannot be reconstructed and are not invented.

Direct models receive `create_goal`, `get_goal`, and `update_goal`. The creation
tool instructs the model to act only on an explicit user request and never adds
a default budget. The update tool can mark only `complete` or genuinely
`blocked`; pause, resume, clear, and limiting states remain user/system
authority. Goal operations still pass through the native prepared-tool and
permission boundary, and never alter the selected local, Podman, or SSH
execution backend.


An explicitly authorized coordinator can also use the native
[`task_goal` peer controls](independent-tasks.md#explicit-peer-goal-controls) on an
independent plain direct Local task. Each peer action needs a separate manual
human authorization and ordinary permission evaluation. This adds no authority
to the target's own `update_goal` tool or to traditional child sessions.

sections.text:
# Heartbeats

An interval or calendar heartbeat returns to the same direct Local chat to check a saved
purpose. Ask the agent explicitly to schedule it, or open the chat's
**Heartbeats** panel and choose **New heartbeat**. The panel also lists schedules
from **All chats** on this serving host. SSH, Podman, delegated and managed-host
execution are not qualified for this initial feature.

sections.title: Scheduling and control
sections.text:
## Scheduling and control

Save the instructions, cadence, finish condition and any installed skill names.
An ordinary check creates neither a goal nor another chat. Optionally bind an
already-active goal in this exact chat; paused, blocked, replaced and exhausted
goals never become active merely because a heartbeat is due.

Choose an elapsed interval, daily local time, selected weekdays, or one weekly
day. Calendar rules always save an explicit IANA timezone, such as
`America/Los_Angeles`. A new form initially captures the viewing device's zone;
review it before saving. The stored zone stays fixed when the device or server
timezone changes. Raw cron/RRULE, monthly/yearly calendars and quiet hours are
not supported.

The form previews upcoming instants both in the stored zone and UTC before
creation or an edit. Native agents use `preview_heartbeat` for the same passive
calculation, then save the returned rule/data version with `heartbeat_control`.
`read_heartbeat` returns the saved rule, exact next due and upcoming UTC/local
instants. Preview and history reads never attach, wake or schedule a chat.

Nonexistent spring-forward wall times are skipped. A repeated wall time fires
once, at its earliest UTC occurrence. Calendar cadence follows local dates, not
an assumed 24-hour elapsed interval. Editing the zone, time or day rule selects
a strictly future point of the new version and withdraws unstarted old work;
already-admitted work keeps its original rule and UTC provenance. Downtime
coalesces into one check with the actual missed UTC range and count. Resume
skips deliberately paused dates, including gaps/folds, and a backward clock
does not rewind the retained next due.

Calendar calculation uses NAC-owned pinned official IANA **2026f** data through
Jiff **0.2.38**, with the MIT license choice and only `std` enabled. No host zone
files, automatic network refresh, bundled fallback or POSIX timezone strings
participate. Every saved calendar rule retains its data version. Unknown zones,
versions or rules fail visibly. A deliberate data update must retain support
for saved versions or explicitly migrate/review affected schedules; it must not
silently reinterpret existing due identities.

Preview contains at most 16 points. Each next/previous search examines at most
366 local dates; downtime counting uses arithmetic weekday totals and at most
32,768 timezone transitions rather than replaying every missed date. Existing
history, start, concurrency and command-receipt limits below also apply to
calendar schedules. This calendar surface targets existing chats. A calendar
with a fresh-task destination is unsupported until the separate ALL-484 integration.

For an elapsed interval, the first check is due one interval after creation.
Later due points stay on that anchor. **Run now** requests a separate occurrence without moving it.
Busy chats retain one pending check per schedule, coalescing the missed range
and count; queued human input gets priority. Editing an interval starts a new
cadence/version and withdraws unstarted old work. **Pause** withdraws pending
work. **Resume** picks a future point on the retained cadence without replaying
paused time. **Stop** also requests cancellation of the exact active check.
**Delete** removes future scheduling while reporting any check already admitted;
it does not claim that active effects were cancelled.

A pending structured question defers a check without spending its occurrence or
retry allowance. After an answer is accepted, its exact reserved continuation
gets priority; the heartbeat cannot consume that response as its own input.

The server owns scheduling from startup, so closing every browser does not stop
checks. Stopping the server stops admission and uses normal run cleanup. After
an interrupted admission or execution, the schedule suspends for review with
its original receipt and run identity. Uncertain effects are never automatically
replayed. Read the evidence before editing or resuming it.

Results retain evidence and a link to their run. An unchanged result stays quiet
in the session list. Meaningful changes, completion, missing classification,
failure and human-action results remain visible until opened. A model report is
provisional: final failure, interruption or a denied action takes precedence.
Human controls do not grant future unattended tool approval; checks use current
agent policy and the backend/workspace selected for this chat.

sections.title: Limits and retained history
sections.text:
## Limits and retained history

The initial finite operating limits are:

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Interval | 60 seconds to 365 days |
| Host schedule inventory, including retained deletion tombstones | 100 |
| Concurrent heartbeat runs per host | 4 |
| Starts per host | 60 per trailing minute |
| Starts per schedule, including Run now | At least 15 seconds apart |
| Pending work | One coalesced occurrence per schedule |
| Retained results | 32 per schedule, plus active/pending work |
| Default checks per schedule | 1,000; configurable from 1 to 100,000 |
| Deadline per check | 300 seconds by default; 1 second to 1 hour |
| Command receipts | 4,096, plus a bounded reserve for remaining pause/stop/delete transitions |

Within the same history allowance, recent admitted starts take precedence over
newer withdrawn requests so trimming cannot erase the start-rate fences.
Only a later admitted start advances that retention window; control and
settlement timestamps cannot expire starts needed after a clock rollback.
If the wall clock falls behind the latest retained host start, heartbeat admission
waits until it catches up. Pending receipt identity and retry allowance stay intact.

An accepted Stop retains its exact-run cancellation request through later edits
or deletion until that occurrence settles. Delete alone does not cancel a run.
Withdrawing unstarted checks does not turn an earlier unchanged result into unread
activity; later ordinary runs and actionable results still remain visible.

Deleting a schedule retains its tombstone and original command responses so a
lost acknowledgement can be retried safely. Capacity exhaustion requires human
review; deletion does not erase those identities. The panel freezes an uncertain
request until **Retry same request** reconciles it. A definite rejection allows
reviewing the latest schedule before issuing another command.

Token allowances stop subsequent admission after settled usage reaches the
allowance, or when usage is unknown. In-flight tokens are not a fabricated final
charge. A running check can overrun a token allowance before its final sample is
known. Deadlines use monotonic elapsed time and request exact-run cancellation;
process cleanup may finish after the deadline. History and usage retain those
facts rather than claiming immediate rollback or a hard provider-token cutoff.
